NSF Grant Proposal Pathways To Cybersecurity Careers Submitted April 2022 The U.S.
Bureau of Labor Statistics predicts the growth in cybersecurity employment demand will be 34% in the near future.
This is projected to cause over 700,000 unfilled cybersecurity jobs in the U.S., costing the U.S. economy billions of dollars.
While there exists this dramatic shortage in the cybersecurity workforce, there is a parallel phenomenon that only 4% of entry level cybersecurity positions currently go to people classified as from low-income backgrounds.
This Track 2 S-STEM project, called Pathways To A Cybersecurity Career (P2CC), will support low-income students to graduate with a Master’s degree in Cybersecurity from the University of Rhode Island (URI), and enter the cybersecurity workforce.
The P2CC project will provide yearly scholarships of 1-3 year durations to at least 42 unique recipients over 6 years, with expected retention and graduation rates being at least 90%.
The scholars will be domestic low-income students with academic ability, talent/potential, and with demonstrated unmet financial need.

They will be recruited by a campaign that targets traditionally under-represented groups in the cybersecurity field including women, rational/ethnic minorities, and differently-abled people.
Selection of scholars will be by a panel that has been trained in potential selection biases when evaluating low-income applicants, using a rubric that is designed for equity.
In addition to providing scholarships, the P2CC project will implement curricular and co-curricular interventions for the scholars that will target cognitive and non-cognitive aspects of low-income students’ experiences and success that focus on academic supports, and on increasing the students’ professional identity through exposure to the cybersecurity workforce and professional skills, professional role modeling, participation in student cohorts, faculty mentoring, and building self efficacy.
Intellectual Merit.
The interventions of the P2CC project will adapt, implement, and study the application to cybersecurity education of evidence-based curricular and co-curricular interventions that have been shown to be effective supporting low-income student recruitment, retention, and success in STEM education.

The P2CC project’s primary intervention uses Fitzgerald’s definition of “professional identity” as: “containing the attributes: skills and functions; knowledge values and ethics; personal identity; group identity in the profession; and the influence of the context of the field”.
It applies to cybersecurity education specific professional identity enhancement techniques that Peters has classified as “high impact” for low-income STEM student success, and that have been demonstrated on similar S-STEM projects in Math, Science, and Computer Science.
The project includes a robust evaluation of its primary objectives: 1) produce at least 42 graduates who enter the cybersecurity workforce, 2) evaluate the effectiveness of the support interventions in supporting the success of low-income cybersecurity students, and 3) disseminate the results to assist degree programs at other institutions in supporting the success of low-income students in their cybersecurity education.
The evaluation uses data sources including pre and post surveys of scholars, exit tickets following specific activities, exit interviews, demographic data, academic assessments, and career placement data.

The evaluation performs formative evaluation of the objectives using a formal Plan-Do-Study-Act continuous improvement process, and summative evaluation to facilitate reporting and academic publication.

Broader Impacts. This project impacts the scholars themselves, all of which will be low-income students, by providing them access to a high-quality graduate education in cybersecurity - something that is unattainable by many due to economic hardship, and the lack of available financial aid at the graduate level. The professional identity and academic enhancement interventions will help ensure the success of these scholars. The broader impact will be on both the U.S. cybersecurity workforce, which lacks numbers and diversity of workers , and on the U.S. economy as a whole. By producing more qualified cybersecurity workers from low-income background, the P2CC project will serve as an initial step in starting to tap a woefully untapped talent pool that will help address a U.S. cybersecurity workforce deficit crisis that is costing billions of dollars in losses to the nation’s economy, and affecting international competitiveness of U.S. companies.
